Large Array found a temporary radio burst, designated Cygnus A-2, emanating from Cygnus A. Given the burst's intense radio output, this transient was thought to likely be a secondary black hole in an orbit with the galaxy's central black hole. Using X-ray data from 2015 to 2017 collected with the Chandra observatory, the research team looked for any matching signal associated with the burst, but found that due to its proximity to the central black hole, any evidence of a secondary black hole would be obscured. As an alternative, the team considered how the burst could have originated from the accretion disk of the primary black hole. In this scenario, the burst would have corresponded to the edge of the disk's shadow, a theory that aligns with other observations of periodic variability. Any evidence of a secondary black hole would need to come from other wavelengths, such as X-ray or radio spectra, and further investigation is needed to confirm the origin of this temporary burst. Essentially, it guarantees that all system members receive the same information, even if certain malicious members deceive others by sending conflicting data. Existing broadcast protocols rely on a central point of trust, with specific groups (quorums) assumed to function reliably. This study focuses on a decentralized model where every participant establishes its own trusted groups (quorums). We introduce a set of relaxed broadcast abstractions tailored to these settings and develop an optimal broadcast protocol, which achieves the highest level of consistency by ensuring system members only receive the same information from a single source. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we find that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates the non-existence of any charged states. As a result, the $\theta$-terms lead to the denial of all universal symmetries within the array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories. This denial also extends to theories derived from string theory that incorporate D-branes with magnetic charges. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the $\theta$-terms act in the denial of universal symmetries and that this denial occurs without relying on the specific characteristics of effective field theories derived from string theory. Rather, the denial occurs due to the presence of the $\theta$-terms which are a characteristic feature of superstring theory. This denial is, therefore, an inherent feature of supergravity theory itself. This denial has implications far beyond the scope of the effective field theories studied

Model uncertainty, also referred to as epistemic uncertainty, is a concept that measures a model's expected prediction error beyond random noise. In this paper, a novel metric called pathwise epistemic uncertainty for estimating Q-value functions is introduced, accompanied by a method for approximating its upper limit known as the F-value. Experimental testing with Deep Q-Networks reveals that measuring uncertainty in reinforcement learning can serve as a reliable indicator of training progress. Building upon this discovery, a novel approach is proposed, Critic Confidence Guided Exploration (CCGE), where an actor-critic algorithm incorporates guidance from an existing oracle policy when the learner is uncertain, minimizing the impact of unnecessary random actions during training. Implementing CCGE on Soft Actor-Critic using the F-value metric in popular Gym environments resulted in improved sample efficiency and higher episodic rewards compared to the original Soft Actor-Critic algorithm. The impact of different model uncertainty estimates is also analyzed, highlighting the significance of accurately calculating uncertainty in reinforcement learning. In saturated saline soils, evaporation causes salts to accumulate at the soil's surface, increasing the liquid's density and creating a gravitationally unstable condition prone to finger formations. These fingers facilitate the downward transport of salt. We are examining the formation of these fingers using both linear stability analysis and numerical simulations. Linear stability analysis determines the instability thresholds across various parameter ranges, while simulations using specific parameters offer insights into finger development after onset. By combining this understanding, we can predict the occurrence and timing of instabilities and their effects on surface salt concentration. This combined approach allows for the prediction of when and where these fingers will appear in the soil surface. Notably, we found that the Lord-Rayleigh instability factor plays a crucial role in this process. When the Lord-Rayleigh number exceeds a certain threshold, known as the critical value, these fingers appear, and we've identified the minimum required for this to happen. As the Lord-Rayleigh number increases beyond this critical value, the amplitude and spatial spacing of these fingers also change. The primary objective of my doctoral research is to streamline this workflow. By developing an automatic method, mathematical expressions can be semantically enhanced for seamless integration into computer algebra systems as well as other platforms such as search engines and plagiarism detection tools, ensuring that essential semantic attributes are maintained during import. Investigating causes of porosity in galvanically coupled aluminum-silicon alloys manufactured using selective laser melting is the focus of this study. To this end, samples produced by two manufacturers were examined for porosity, and their microstructures, phase compositions, and stress states were studied. Notably, significant amounts of porosity were observed in manufactured samples, particularly in the aluminum phase, and further analysis revealed the onset of plastic deformation in the aluminum phase and the emergence of voids during continued solidification. Future research directions involving predictive models and experimental methods to forecast and prevent porosity are outlined. Since porosity is inherent in additive manufacturing of aluminum-silicon alloys, understanding its causes and potential remedies is crucial for optimizing and facilitating the development of useful aluminum-silicon alloy parts.

Our investigation explores the merits and complexities of employing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in classification tasks, especially those requiring event selection. This research aims to tackle the difficult challenge of protecting IoT data privacy by employing an advanced statistical technique: inference testing. Ultimately, we outline avenues for future exploration, considering the inherent complexities of IoT data and the need for enhanced privacy protection.

fields of machine learning appear stagnant, despite claims of progress being published in the literature. A major factor contributing to the lack of progress is the non-verifiable nature of model comparison studies. These studies often overlook established causes of unreliability, which hampers third-party validation of results. To shed light on the problem, we aimed to gather insights from existing research, gather original data, and employ statistical analysis to shed light on the underlying causes. A survey with 112 participants from the machine learning community was conducted, along with an analysis of 107,000 code repositories. Our findings reveal that the most concerning issues are a lack of reproducibility, poor documentation, and inadequate reporting of studies. A notable finding is that these concerns are more prevalent in areas experiencing perceived stagnation, such as recommender systems and semantic segmentation. Our work suggests addressing these issues could unlock new areas of research and revive dormant areas, potentially leading to improved model comparison studies and the advancement of the field as a whole. The survey and code repositories can be found at https://github.com/m-l-Forbes/ml-stagnation. Structural influence and the potential for confirmation bias are explored in the technical report at https://m-l-forbes.github.io/stagnation-report.html. Known by various names globally including Industrie 4.0 in Germany and industrial internet in the US, initiatives aimed at promoting digitization are gaining momentum, but specific implementation details remain unclear.  To bridge this knowledge gap, Germany's Industry 4.0 initiative introduced the Reference Architecture Model (RAM) as a comprehensive framework.  However, the English-language documentation for RAM is scarce, potentially hindering understanding among English-speaking manufacturers.  To address this, a new study translates key Industry 4.0 documents into English and uses RAM as a foundation to develop an explanatory overview.  The results are then presented in a comprehensive paper, providing newcomers with a clear understanding of RAM and its components.  The paper also offers original content to facilitate seamless reference to Industry 4.0 best practices and guidelines.  The study aims to provide engineers and researchers with the knowledge needed to effectively implement RAM and support digital transformation initiatives.  The results can serve as a starting point or precursor to other studies, enabling researchers to investigate specific aspects of RAM and contribute to the growing body of Industry 4.0 knowledge.  The research outcomes include two English-language documents - a overview and a guide - available online for public access.

We achieve this by converting each ad into a set of visual identifiers that reflect its content. These identifiers are then used to generate visual embeddings, which can improve CTR predictions. In order to address these limitations, a new tracking method called Multiple Hypothesis Hypergraph Tracking (MHHT) has been developed. MHHT leverages hypergraphs to capture the interconnected movement of objects, making it more effective at tracking objects even in the most demanding scenarios. MHHT's versatility is showcased through its application in tracking individual seam cells during the late stages of an embryo's development in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Extension of MHHT's algorithm is also possible using a variety of methods such as parameter adjustment, incorporating external object information, or utilizing hypergraph contraction to optimize performance. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. A thorough evaluation involved over one hundred DepAD variants across 32 real-world datasets to assess the efficacy of representative techniques. Notably, experiments demonstrated that DepAD consistently outperformed state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods in a wide range of scenarios. The proposed framework serves as a foundation for future research on dependency-based anomaly detection, providing a benchmark for evaluation. The code and results are publicly available for replication and further investigation. This research was supported by the Australian Government through the Australian Research Council and by MSRA. An essential component for constructing large-scale integrated quantum networks is an integrated quantum memory for polarization qubits. Yet, efficiently storing these qubits over extended periods requires accounting for factors like optical loss, spontaneous emission, and qubit lifetime variability due to material imperfections. Research on integrated quantum memory for polarization qubits is notably absent in previous studies. To bridge this knowledge gap, we propose a method to develop such a memory using a monolithic silicon photonic device, featuring a resonant cavity and integrated thermo-optic switch. An intrinsic broadband silicon waveguide serves as the cavity and combines with the thermo-optic switch to achieve single-photon storage with high efficiency. Using this design, we achieve a 0.71+-0.04 gate efficiency, surpassing previous silicon-based approaches. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to store single photons for 8.8+-0.2 nanoseconds, enable the detection of multiple photons within 2.4 nanoseconds, and achieve a high storage fidelity for polarization-encoded quantum bits. This design yields a high optical loss tolerance and reduces material limitations, paving the way for efficient storage of polarization qubits. Notably, it offers a promising pathway for constructing large-scale integrated quantum networks with minimal loss of photon signal. This innovation has significant potential to advance the development of quantum computation and communication over long-distance channels. , such as supply chain finance and digital governance, has highlighted the importance of confidential smart contracts in practical applications. However, the emerging need for privacy protection techniques in smart contracts remains inadequately addressed. Specifically, the feasibility of securely implementing Multi-party Computation (MPC) in smart contracts remains understudied, particularly with respect to the trade-offs of cost, flexibility, and security. This paper proposes TENET, a modular and adaptable framework for confidential smart contracts that leverages a trusted execution environment (TEE) network to address the challenges of supporting MPC-enabled contracts in a secure and efficient manner. Key features of TENET include anonymous MPC negotiation, atomic and fair output distribution, and constant transaction overhead. Our results show that TENET can achieve MPC security with only three transactions and outperform state-of-the-art solutions in both theoretical and practical evaluations, involving scenarios with two to eleven parties, at a cost that is 0.55 to 0.98 times the baseline (with an average of 0.91 times the baseline). The TENET framework, which consists of 3,410 lines of code, is open-source and available on GitHub. This work is innovative because it is the first to implement a confidential smart contract framework in Rust, addressing a pressing need in the blockchain community, and demonstrating the feasibility of securely evaluating any program with MPC at a reasonable cost. The TENET framework has received attention from 62 practitioners and researchers, who viewed it as useful for supporting confidential smart contracts

While ParVI methods generally do not permit unconstrained posterior sampling, certain approaches suffer from suboptimal results.  This work develops a novel approach that empowers learning to sample from a posterior distribution with high accuracy.  We propose constructing a neural network sampler optimized using the gradients of the KL-divergence between a predicted posterior and a sampled distribution.  This generative ParVI method, or GPVI, can be viewed as an extension of previous generative ParVI methods, which we demonstrate through analysis and empirical studies in Bayesian linear regression and hidden Markov models.  GPVI achieves state-of-the-art results in approximating the posterior distribution and performs significantly better in scenarios where posterior sampling is essential.  We also note that GPVI shares similarities with previous generative ParVI methods in that both predict a latent variable distribution jointly with a task-specific quantity, such as the data or observations.  Consequently, we suggest the term 'auxiliary generative ParVI' to describe methods like GPVI that predict an auxiliary quantity separately, like the inclusion status of latent variables in hidden Markov models.  This distinction highlights the diversity in ParVI methods and contributes to a clearer understanding of the field.  All code for GPVI is available at https://github.com/phoenix92/GPVI. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with class-balanced regularization in the model re-training process. Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of object detection and highlights its limitations. Notably, FPN tends to suffer from significant object size constraints, largely resulting from the inherent drawback inherent to the framework. This paper proposes the Scale Pyramid Selection (SPS) module to address two key issues associated with object detection within crowded scenes and large-scale objects. Firstly, SPS enhances the detailed spatial analysis of objects by addressing the under-constrained issues associated with object size constraints. Secondly, SPS identifies and mitigates overlapping pyramid levels to eliminate unnecessary feature down-sampling caused by object size constraints. We evaluate our proposed method against current state-of-the-art object detection frameworks on the COCO dataset and find that it surpasses these benchmarks by a significant margin, achieving improved performance in both crowd scene and general object detection scenarios. Our method can be integrated seamlessly with existing object detection frameworks. Notably, integration of SPS with two prominent object detection methods yields improved performance, with a notable 2.3% and 1.4% improvement in the crowd scenario and general object detection scenario respectively. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and speed, paving the way for the efficient assembly of large genomes. By exploiting parallel processing and advanced data structures, the assembly process is substantially accelerated, enabling the direct construction of complete genomes from sequenced nucleotides within a chromosomal region. This innovative assembly method seamlessly integrates with existing genome annotation tools and demonstrates superior accuracy over established algorithms, particularly in the assembly of large and repetitive genomes. Furthermore, the algorithm's parameter settings are analyzed, showcasing the correlation between genome complexity, sequence lengths, and the optimal assembly parameters.

This complex phenomenon, present in most superconductors with a long-range order, has not been thoroughly explained, hindering efforts to identify its underlying causes. In the case of BSCCO thin films, researchers have suggested that grain-boundary driven vortices may be responsible for the positive Hall resistivity observed near the vortex-liquid phase transition. However, a critical aspect emerged - the presence of positive Hall resistivity in BSCCO thin films was only accompanied by a signature of the phase transition, marked by a distinctive 'kink', in their mixed-state Hall conductivity. This discovery led to a re-evaluation of previous measurements, revealing a critical finding - the positive Hall resistivity anomaly could be attributed to an intrinsic electronic scattering process affecting under-confining grain-boundary vortices. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the vortex electronic scattering process interacts with the confining potential near the outer vortex edge, producing a modulation of the scattering rate. This, in turn, produces the observed 'kink' signature in the mixed-state Hall conductivity. Based on these insights, we propose that the positive Hall resistivity anomaly is a universal phenomenon in iiSCs, supported by additional experimental evidence from CaBreaker. This understanding of the anomaly not only resolves the previously reported discrepancies but also sheds new light on the vortex electronic scattering process and its interaction with confining potentials near vortex edges

This study examines how GAN training is affected by high-frequency components.
During the typical GAN training process, significant high-frequency differences compel the discriminator to excessively focus on high-frequency features.
This issue restricts the generator from capturing the low-frequency features critical to capturing the image content.
We present two straightforward yet effective techniques to mitigate these adverse effects:
High-Frequency Confusion (HFC) and High-Frequency Filter (HFF).
These techniques are versatile and can be applied to various GAN architectures at no additional cost.
The superior performance of our techniques is confirmed on multiple performance metrics, architectures, and datasets.
Specifically, the HFF approach leads to notable enhancements of 42.5%, 30.2%, and 69.3% in the FID metric for SNGAN, SSGAN, and InfoMAXGAN respectively when generating high-quality images on CelebA. The source code is available at https://github.com/ghm0x80/High-Frequency-GAN.

In future quantum networks, we need to overcome inherent limitations stemming from the probabilistic emission of photons by utilizing predictable quantum light sources. Emerging research suggests that confined electron-hole pairs within ultra-thin solid-state materials can be leveraged for generating quantum light. These novel emitters hold great promise as solid-state realizations of two-level systems, offering potential applications in the development of quantum processors and quantum networks. This study aims to explore their potential in enabling reliable quantum communication by utilizing a confined electron-hole system as a model to demonstrate the principles of quantum key distribution. By projecting an input state onto this emitter and employing a single-photon detector to detect coherent superposition states, we develop an analytical framework to assess the key exchange rate. Our analysis further considers how to differentiate signal from background noise by utilizing the non-markovian behavior of the coherent evanescent electric field surrounding the emitter, thereby enabling the optimization of secret key extraction. This analysis demonstrates that specific conditions are required for reliable quantum key distribution and identifies limitations arising from the coherent evanescent electric field. These constraints, however, can be mitigated through the implementation of a double-edge structure that eliminates coherent electron-hole interactions, thus enabling the achievement of optimal secret key extraction rates. These findings indicate the feasibility of using these novel emitters for conducting reliable quantum key distribution experiments. This analysis provides a valuable foundation for exploring quantum key distribution applications within the context of future solid-state quantum processors and quantum networks.

DeepMoCap, employs a combination of infrared-depth sensors, reflective markers, and machine learning algorithms to automatically capture motion. This is achieved through the use of a non-parametric representation and a multi-stage fully convolutional network to jointly estimate marker 3D positions and temporal smoothing. In conjunction with two cost functions, DeepMoCap generates a motion capture solution. This is further enhanced by integrating a non-parametric soft-body model to improve capture quality and robustness in various scenarios, including the capture of complex dynamic movements and motions under varying lighting conditions. Results demonstrate DeepMoCap's effectiveness in capturing high-quality motion without the need for parameterized models or precise initial alignment. This is evident in its performance across multiple datasets and the capture of indeterminate movements. Due to its reliance on depth sensors and reflective markers, DeepMoCap is suitable for capture sessions within indoor environments and can be extended to use other depth-sensing technologies, such as LiDAR and RGB-D cameras, through the substitution of optical sensors and marker adaptation. With its capacity to capture motion anonymously and efficiently, DeepMoCap presents numerous applications in various fields, including computer science and social sciences. This approach offers a motion capture tool that can be utilized in multiple disciplines, including social sciences and computer science. Given its anonymity and speed, DeepMoCap has significant practical implications. This paper documents multiple experiments conducted to evaluate DeepMoCap's performance. Results demonstrate that DeepMoCap outperforms current state-of-the-art motion capture methods,

Our framework consists of a sequence of connected modules, enabling the calculation of the normalising constant for each module and its sub-modules. Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. A more efficient variant of this estimator, tailored to the sketch size parameter d, reduces the query complexity to O(d/k^2), outperforming all existing safe estimators for d >= k^2. Auto-tuning computer systems is a complex process requiring significant resources and time. Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO) has been successful in this area but has a limitation: it requires expert-provided system structures which can be difficult to obtain. Our research addresses this issue by presenting BoAnon, an SBO framework that discovers system structures from logs and uses this information to optimize performance. BoAnon identifies meaningful structures and leverages expert knowledge to boost optimization efficiency. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this layer, a novel two-stage learning algorithm has been designed, ensuring that the constructed problem is always feasible. We examine the unification of eight major global pooling methods, including average, min, max, topk, and attention pooling. To evaluate the performance of UOTP, a series of experiments were conducted on multiple large-scale image classification datasets. The results indicate that UOTP consistently outperforms traditional global pooling methods and other state-of-the-art models, such as ResNet-101 and SeNet-153. Furthermore, a substantial increase in UOTP's training flexibility was observed, allowing it to be easily integrated with other deep learning architectures. Consequently, a publicly accessible UOTP code, known as Squeeze-Dense Unit via Optimal Transport, has been made available for use in the development of more efficient global pooling layers. has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications are hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable to execute within time constraints.  To address these challenges, a new quality assessment approach for Linked Data has been proposed, centered on a novel framework called LDFinder that efficiently identifies and scores data issues on a large scale.  This new approach, implemented in the LDFinder tool and evaluated on a comprehensive data set, surpasses existing techniques in both precision and scalability.  As a result, higher-quality data can now be achieved, enabling more reliable data-driven applications and solutions.  The LDFinder tool and its accompanying evaluations can be found at https://lod2rdf.info/ldfinder.  Additionally, a new dataset comprising annotated data from various Linked Data sets, created to support the evaluations and foster further research, is available at http://purl.org/mydata/ldquality.  This work has been presented at the 11th Extended Semantic Web Conference, which took place in June 2018 in Montpellier, France.  This research was undertaken with the financial support of the EU's FP7 project LOD2.

Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using pre-defined rules, but these methods fail to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions. In contrast, inverse reinforcement learning holds promise for more sophisticated scenario generation. Nonetheless, this method is hampered by requirements for explicit reward functions and data availability. Building upon these limitations, a novel approach has been developed to automate scenario creation: an agent is trained to mimic a human driver's behavior, and their path is then followed in a empty environment to create a traffic scenario. The method's effectiveness was tested using a widely used driving simulator; it outperformed traditional approaches in scenario complexity and realism ratings, as verified by human evaluators. Furthermore, this approach demonstrated better controller stability and closer proximity to human trajectory data in diverse driving scenarios. Although initial results indicate promise, the method's reliance on extensive offline training data means it may not be suitable for immediate deployment in testing and validation processes. In light of this, future work could focus on adapting this method for real-world applications, such as predictive vehicle control. In this context, incorporating an optimistic planner to guide the vehicle towards a safe and realistic scenario, as determined by human experts, could yield better results. Ultimately, this approach offers a promising solution for creating realistic traffic scenarios that mimic actual driving conditions. When combined with predictive techniques, it holds potential for significant applications in autonomous driving research and development. The analysis yielded a catalog of 2034 Corona Australis members, including 1328 that received spectroscopic classification in this research. Our findings reveal that the Corona Australis cluster is comprised of two distinct stellar populations: one young (approximately a few million years) embedded within the cloud and the Coronet Cluster, and a second older population (~15 million years) surrounding and extending beyond the cloud in the Upper Corona Australis region. Furthermore, the distribution of spectral types in Corona Australis reaches a peak at M5 (~0.15 solar mass), suggesting that the Initial Mass Function of Corona Australis is consistent with that of nearby star-forming regions in the vicinity of the Upper Corona Australis region. Our findings specify the following: for a treewidth-r graph, there exist multipliers such that the ratio of the max-flow and min-cut values is no more than r times better than the optimal ratio. cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine the collision in a finite system using properties of compact objects. We model the particle cloud as a cooling gas whose thermal energy diminishes until it reaches the black hole's event horizon. We derive a set of self-similar solutions characteristic of this process and introduce a key parameter governing the speed of the particle cloud as it converges on the black hole. We find that, depending on the mass of the particle cloud, there are two distinct solutions, each corresponding to different initial velocities of the cloud. When the mass of the particle cloud exceeds a certain threshold, the solutions indicate that the collision results in a shockwave forming just beyond the black hole's event horizon. In contrast, a massless particle cloud produces solutions devoid of shockwaves, with the solutions instead indicating the gradual accretion of the cloud by the black hole. We calculate the point at which the shockwave begins and find that its location varies significantly based on the parameters of the collision, including the speed of the particle cloud. We propose that the distance of the shockwave from the event horizon could be used to distinguish between shockwave and non-shockwave collisions using observations of gravitational waves. We further find that, in the vicinity of the shockwave, the solutions obey a specific scaling law governing the acceleration of the particle cloud, a phenomenon we term the 'acceleration singularity.' unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects. Firstly, we reevaluate the previous unclonable encryption construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, considering only secure protocols that rely on computational problems that require significant computational power to solve. We find that this construction includes two distinct encryption processes and has a limited range of possible input data. We then create new unclonable encryption constructions, both basic and advanced, using established secure protocols. Our work also explores the possibility of creating an unclonable encryption scheme that allows a limited number of attempts to clone data, a concept known as $k$-times clonable encryption. We establish the requirements for secure $k$-times clonable encryption schemes and create an example of this type using the learning with errors problem. We also examine the possibility of creating an unclonable encryption scheme that allows an adversary to clone data multiple times in a short time frame after a initial non-influential action, a concept known as a one-time clocking unclonable encryption scheme. we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole as stipulated by the standard extremality threshold, the perturbation must violate the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and used them to determine the extremality threshold for such black holes. This method can be extended to compute corrections for more complex solutions and will be valuable in identifying the threshold at which black holes become unstable. Our findings indicate that time series containing significant event interdependence tend to exhibit higher instances of rare events compared to those following traditional Gaussian distributions. These infrequent events are significantly underpredicted by the Gaussian model, known as the "tail risk gap," and can be quantified by the difference between the 97th percentile of the log-return distribution and the corresponding 97th percentile of a generalized Pareto distribution fitted to the non-Gaussian excess. Our analysis shows that this "tail risk gap" diminishes as the event dependence lessens, ultimately dropping to negligible levels in Gaussian cases. To measure the degree of event interdependence, we employed two methods: one relying on the independence threshold from linear regression analysis and the other determining the degree of event interdependence based on the precision matrix of a modified multivariate normal distribution that accommodates cointegration. Our analysis also explores the impact of event interdependence on the Calpheon measure, revealing that it tends to overstate the likelihood of rare events when the time series exhibits high event interdependence. Conversely, this overstatement decreases as the event interdependence lessens. The Calpheon measure's accuracy in capturing the non-Gaussian behavior peaks at intermediate levels of event interdependence. The significance of understanding "tail risk gap" lies in its implications for the management of financial risk, as recognizing non-Gaussian event interdependence can lead to more effective risk mitigation strategies, regardless of the degree of interdependence

However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing intrinsic network features, we create a comprehensive, descriptive verbal explanation of a DNN's decision rationale through an analysis of learned features, associated human-interpretable concepts, and an ILP approach resulting in logical rules that faithfully mirror the behavior of the original complex model. The implementation details are made publicly accessible on GitHub. The outcome is that our method successfully recreates the decision logic of a sophisticated DNN with precision, and we demonstrate its efficacy with rigorous evaluation on benchmarks and real-world images. Moreover, we show that our explanation, generated solely from visual data, achieves high accuracy when tested on the benchmark MIMVAC dataset, using a distance metric tailored to accommodate feature sets with varying sizes. Crucially, the natural language explanations generated by our method are also superior to other state-of-the-art explanations, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Finally, we highlight a significant practical advantage: Unlike other explanation techniques, our method allows the incorporation of intrinsic network features without manual annotation, making it suitable for a wider range of tasks and applications.

Caching content at network edge in a proactive manner, while considering the interconnectedness of social networks, appears as a viable option to mitigate this problem. Our proposal is Bingo, a content caching scheme that capitalizes on online social networks' interest-based group structures. Our study further examines the impact of different scarcity metrics and user behavior patterns on Bingo's performance and finds that it performs best under conditions characterized by heavy content sharing and clear indicators of future user demands. The growth function of any algebra with a finite number of generators, which is also infinite in size, will naturally follow an increasing and submultiplicative pattern.
The extent to which the previously-mentioned growth function criteria (increasing and submultiplicative) act as a complete set of necessary conditions was a subject posed and explored by numerous authors, prompting a great deal of research in this area.
We discovered that there are arbitrarily rapid functions that satisfy the increasing and submultiplicative criteria yet are not representable as a growth function for any algebra, thus solving a particular problem first introduced by Zelmanov (later reiterated by Alahmadi-Alsulami-Jain-Zelmanov).
In the space of growth functions, we identify the $L$-classes as equivalence relationships based on the notion of "algebraically similar" as per the notion of algebraic depth introduced by Alahmadi-Alsulami-Jain-Zelmanov.
We demonstrate the $L$-classes to be maximal classes that are closed under taking subalgebras, derive combinatorial descriptions for each of the lower $L$-classes, and show that growth functions belonging to the upper $L$-classes can be expressed as a product of functions from specific, smaller $L$-classes.

Notably, the quantum computer's architecture plays a significant role in determining the circuit's performance. \\

Early exit (EE) techniques address these concerns by dynamically streamlining computations for individual samples at inference time, though this approach has been more limitedly applied in sequence-to-sequence speech recognition tasks due to issues of degraded intermediate outputs. Due to the varied appearances of tumors, segmentation can be a difficult task.  Currently, semi-supervised methods that utilize both tumor masks and regional metrics experience limitations in handling diverse tumor appearances.  This research introduces a new approach called Multivariate Activation-Based Brain Tumor Segmentation (MABS), which leverages image activation and multivariate metrics derived from regional feature analysis to improve tumor segmentation.  MABS employs a dual-cost optimization process that balances image and multivariate metrics for accurate segmentation.  Experimental results on the BRATS 2020 dataset demonstrate MABS' performance on multiple MRI modalities and its robustness in handling various tumor types.  MABS achieved a 0.379 DICE score, which ranks 6th among 43 competitors in the BRATS 2020 challenge.  Source code and model information are publicly available at https://github.com/ashwinhanumiah/MABS.  This technology has potential applications in image analysis and brain tumor segmentation. This research has significant implications for brain tumor segmentation.

Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics. To achieve this, a systematic analysis of existing research on collaborative tagging systems was conducted, followed by a detailed examination of 12 prominent systems with a history dating back to 2005. The results show that the majority of these systems are no longer actively maintained, with the content creation process often being solely driven by automated means. Furthermore, social interactions are generally limited to user-generated content submission, rather than collaborative behavior. To ensure the validity of these findings, all used data and the underlying analysis code were made publicly available, providing a foundation for future research in this field. Based on this analysis, several recommendations for designing and maintaining functional collaborative tagging systems are presented, including the importance of clear system definitions, ongoing administration, and the integration of social features to facilitate actual collaborative behavior. Additionally, potential applications of these designs, such as the enhancement of existing systems or the development of new systems in emerging fields like the Internet of Things, are explored, with a view to contributing to the ongoing discussion on the design of collaborative tagging systems

Maps with a higher degree of differentiability are more desirable due to their greater analytical capabilities. However, these smoothable structures often retain key characteristics even after being embedded in higher-dimensional spaces. Many of the important factors and time intervals in surgical procedures are often ignored. Unfortunately, deep learning models often lack transparency, making it difficult for doctors to make sense of their predictions. However, feature importance can be used to explain the predictions of a certain model by measuring the influence of specific data features on its performance. Research has shown that feature importance can be used to improve the accuracy of medical predictions by revealing the relationships between certain data features and outcomes. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel, open-world prediction approach called energy calibration, which is characterized by unbounded energy scores and corresponding probabilities greater than one. We also develop a second metric - the distance to positive infinity, d - as a practical indicator of calibration for models employing energy calibration. By employing $d$, we select the best model and hyperparameters for tasks, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving better results in terms of $d$ and overall classification accuracy, compared to conventional methods. Many scenarios, such as working with type-specific Abstract Syntax Trees, inherently involve both pattern matching and generic hierarchies, necessitating proper compiler support. Compilers can address this problem by incorporating subtyping reconstruction: the ability to revive subtyping information that arises during pattern matching runtime. A new theoretical framework, cDOT, is developed to serve as the basis for such a subtyping reconstruction system. As cDOT inherits properties from pDOT, which underpins Scala, it is capable of encapsulating complex features including inheritance with generic types, type constructor variance, type-bound polymorphism, and module recursion. Furthermore, subtyping reconstruction within cDOT encompasses Generalised Algebraic Data Types by encoding $\lambda_{2,G\mu}$ into its structure. A proposed subtyping reconstruction system for a compiler is theoretically justified within the cDOT framework. In addition, an implementation-based approach is presented, where subtyping reconstruction is achieved through type inference and a flexible concept called environmental types, allowing for accurate recovery of original program subtyping relationships. Both approaches are compared, with results indicating that the theoretical framework maintains consistency with the implemented method. An experimental evaluation of the proposed subtyping reconstruction system demonstrates its effectiveness in reviving subtyping information for a variety of practical programs, including full-scale benchmarks like Scala and Rust compilers. forecast intervals and predictive distributions, with the latter viewed as

The conventional notion of accuracy, rooted in mean squared error, is, 
however, incompatible with the fuzzy nature of forecasts, leading to the
definition of a revised accuracy metric grounded in f-divergences for
distributive forecasting. By adopting this perspective, we can ensure the
inclusive application of accuracy metrics to various forecast types and
establish a universal framework for comparing their effectiveness. 
Moreover, our findings imply that precise forecast intervals do not necessarily
correspond to improved accuracy, and that postulating confidence in
probabilityistic forecasts is a somewhat arbitrary position. Ultimately, we
conclude that the choice of accuracy metric is intrinsic to the specific
forecast type and task.

A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network usage, primarily by reducing the amount of data transmitted between base stations. This can be achieved through a joint caching strategy, where the base stations share knowledge of a global cache to optimize both local and remote caching. In this context, a new hierarchical mixed-integer linear program is proposed, designed to determine the most effective joint caching strategy, taking into account both pure caching and computation scenarios. This program ensures optimal performance but due to its complexity, a new efficient two-stage scheme is developed, first identifying the most efficient remote caching allocation, then determining the most effective local caching strategy. This scheme preserves optimal performance in pure caching scenarios, while achieving near optimal results in computation scenarios. Furthermore, a new online approach, inspired by fractional programming, is developed to determine a joint caching strategy, taking into account limited knowledge of user demands at base stations. This approach, outperforming existing solutions, achieves nearly 100% of the best offline solution's effectiveness. Finally, a new hierarchical subproblem is developed to determine a novel split ratio, dividing users into distinct categories, allowing for an improvement of over 90% of the best existing solution. This improved solution, outperforming existing solutions, achieves results close to theoretical limits in both pure caching and computation scenarios. This research contributes to an understanding of the interconnection between caching and computation, providing new efficient solutions to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network usage. In biology, information that's passed on is tricky to spot in pre-biotic systems described through chemical and physical principles. Studying complex systems that store information through time, even if they don't last long, can offer clues. We use computer simulations to investigate systems that transfer information from one generation to the next, focusing on how heritable information arises, persists, and changes over generations. We observe that durable materials with diverse properties can store information in the form of their material ancestry trees. We also found that conserving information often involves decreasing the number of variables. We identified several factors that contribute to heritable information, including fluctuations, the cost of altering existing structures, and the limitations of replicating systems. We discovered that heritable information can emerge spontaneously and persist over thousands of generations, sometimes increasing when the number of variables decreases, a phenomenon that resembles the effect of genetic reduction on evolution's pace. We found that material systems with persistent heritable information are often characterized by their lack of homogeneity on multiple scales, complex responses to external forces, and the production of similar patterns in response to changing conditions, known as class I bifurcations. We found that heritable information can be linked to the decrease in free energy that drives chemical reactions, and limitations on information that can be transmitted through mechanisms like template-based copying. Finally, it provides a foundational understanding of RNA virus evolution, including implications for gene expression, replication, and virus life cycles. The four pillars of Confident AI comprise Repeatability, Believability, Sufficiency, and Adaptability. Each pillar is utilized to investigate underlying challenges in existing AI/ML systems and collectively offer a comprehensive approach to constructing reliable AI models. Specifically, we use the lens of Repeatability to examine issues in predicting chaotic weather patterns and unstable dynamical systems. We focus on Believability to analyze concerns in AI-powered forensic analysis and expert system decision-making. We select Sufficiency to explore problems in ranking lists and condensed summary generation and consider Adaptability in studying evolving classification and dynamic prediction tasks. Our analysis within each confidence dimension encompasses additional insights related to model evaluation, data quality, dataset design, and dataset representation. Ultimately, we propose that the Confident AI framework and its individual pillars can serve as a guiding force for developing and evaluating robust AI models.

The experiment used sealed water phantoms, created through 3D printing, that were exposed to X-rays, protons, and carbon ions at varying intensities up to 340 Gy per second. Oxygen levels were measured using an optical sensor that enabled non-invasive detection. The results revealed that oxygen consumption is solely dependent on the radiation's dose, rate, and energy transfer. Oxygen levels decreased by 0.04-0.18 percent per 10 Gy for 225-kV X-rays, 0.04-0.25 percent per 10 Gy for 224 MeV protons, and 0.09-0.17 percent per 10 Gy for carbon ions. Oxygen consumption slowed as the radiation intensity increased, due to the self-interactions of radicals at higher dose rates, resulting in reduced oxygen consumption at these higher rates. The researchers also found that clinical doses did not completely deplete oxygen levels, even at 10 Gy dose delivery. Ultimately, the study concluded that Flash radiation does deplete oxygen but not to the point of total depletion, with higher dose rates actually resulting in lower oxygen consumption than standard radiotherapy rates. The researchers also discovered that predictive models using data from clinical radiotherapy conditions accurately forecast oxygen consumption at higher dose rates. The study has important implications for the use of FLASH radiation in treating tumors that require high doses of radiation. The researchers also suggested further experimental investigation

This led them to hypothesize that contractible graphs should also have a linear number of edges. This conjecture is proven to be false, and we present counterexamples that demonstrate the converse: graphs with a linear number of edges can be contractible. This finding reveals that the class of contractible graphs is diverse, encompassing a wide range of graphs characterized by their contraction properties. This discovery also raises questions about the durability of other graph invariants and we examine whether the chromatic number is an example. Specifically, we investigate whether contractible graphs have a bounded chromatic number and provide evidence that suggests they do. This finding motivates the conjecture that contractible bipartite graphs have a linearly bounded chromatic number. We provide partial support for this conjecture, showing that this is true for contractible graphs with specific properties and also for a broader class of graphs that include those that can be formed from contractible components. This finding is consistent with previous research and we use it to demonstrate that the chromatic number of contractible graphs can increase exponentially when allowing for splits as well as edge and vertex contractions. This discovery highlights the distinct differences between splits and edge contractions in the context of contractible graphs. When using formal techniques to create such systems, it often becomes challenging to evaluate the overall system behavior due to its enormous size. In this research, we apply a novel approach to streamline model assessment for large-scale systems featuring repeated patterns. the presence of a finite baryon chemical potential has often been used to bypass a well-known limitation of Lattice QCD known as the sign problem. Given the complexity and precision issues associated with calculating higher-order terms, developing various resummation methods has become crucial in minimizing computational costs while producing accurate thermodynamic estimates. A recent breakthrough presented a resummation method to all orders of the chemical potential by incorporating charge density correlation functions into the Taylor series. However, since these correlation functions are calculated stochastically from various random volume sources, biased estimates arise which significantly skew results, especially for large values of the number of correlation functions and the chemical potential. Moreover, at lower temperatures, certain higher-order derivatives of the free energy become distorted. This research provides a cumulant expansion procedure that addresses and rectifies biased estimates by capturing genuine stochastic fluctuations in the correlation functions. A revised formalism is also developed, allowing the exact reproduction of the Taylor series to a specified order of the chemical potential. However, analyzing these numerous flares is a significant task, requiring substantial time and resources. To address this issue, we have developed an automated algorithm to identify stellar flares in TESS data using a template-based approach. This technique involves comparing real-time baseline flux values against historical stellar flare data, which generates a flare index that indicates the likelihood and magnitude of a flare. This index is then used to flag potential flares in the TESS data. This algorithm is currently being utilized to identify stellar flares in TESS data online in real-time. Additionally, we have made our flare data and code available for other purposes. has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its development.  Many scholars, such as Arthur Beicher, have argued that a non-standard analysis-based representation of calculus is grounded in a logical sequence of events.  In this essay, we present an alternative evaluation of Beicher's account, contending that it is built upon a flawed premise regarding the meaning of 'non-standard analysis'.  We propose that Beicher's account is rooted in a standard model of analysis that incorporates infinitesimal numbers, rather than a logical sequence of events.  We argue that the core challenge in defining the logical order of non-standard analysis revolves around formulating a coherent theory of time.  Infinitesimal-based representation of calculus offers a more plausible solution to this challenge.  We draw on the work of philosophers such as Isaac Newton, William Harvey, and James Gregory, as well as contemporary scientists, to illustrate the plausibility of such a model.  Ultimately, we contend that Beicher's account is irrelevant to the task of describing the development of calculus, given its reliance on a model of time that is incompatible with the evidence.  In light of this finding, we advocate for the acceptance of a wide range of mathematical models that are grounded in the physical world, rather than a strict adherence to a single logical order of eventuation.  We also propose the establishment of a new field, 'physical eventuation theory', dedicated to examining the physical bases of time and its implications on the development of mathematics.

stochastic matching and revenue management involves assuming that demand arises from a fixed sequence of unknown item types drawn independently, implying relatively low variance in demand and approximately Poisson distribution. Consequently, matching policies are usually formulated using fluid LPs that only consider the expected demand. However, this paper explores alternative stochastic models for online matching that account for nonparametric and higher variance demand distributions without restrictive assumptions about serial independence. It proposes two new models: \Indep and \Correl, that differ in their assumption regarding the independence of future demands. The \Indep model treats future demands as nonparametric and independent, while the \Correl model incorporates the correlation of demands with past information. These models are capable of representing any distribution of demand and can precisely solve the stochastic matching problem through fluid LPs with relaxed integrality constraints. By sampling from the conditional distribution of remaining demand after each match, the models achieve approximate optimality and logarithmic regret within a factor of O(k), where k is the number of items. Furthermore, when demands are identically and independently distributed, the models offer guaranteed performance with regret limited to O(\sqrt{k}). Notably, these bounds exceed those for the classic \(\epsilon\)-approximation guarantee by a factor of O(k). While this compromise may seem significant, it enables matching policies that account for nonparametric and higher variance demand distributions, which cannot be achieved using existing models and their resulting fluid LPs with only limited integrality constraints. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovation, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. You can access our dataset, code, and model checkpoints at: https://github.com/alan-ai/condaqa. Lastly, we invite you to join a discussion on our dataset, sharing your thoughts

Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash. Through comprehensive benchmarks, we demonstrate that our runtime library yields exceptional performance, as it outperforms alternative methods by up to three orders of magnitude in some cases. Our fault-tolerant runtime library, along with the comprehensive benchmarking results, are publicly available at: https://github.com/parscal/libftor.

A comprehensive simulation framework evaluates the effectiveness of BDI-based solutions in addressing complex D2D challenges. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that BDI-agent solutions can boost D2D link quality, minimize end-users' power consumption, and increase overall network data transfer rates. Consequently, this approach presents a promising solution for tackling complex D2D problems and enables more efficient D2D system design. Building upon these findings, possible directions for future research are explored, including the integration of BDI-based solutions with diverse applications such as content sharing and IoT systems. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. To address this, a novel method utilizing an osmotic mechanism is introduced to accelerate the release of solutes from a spherical capsule. By applying external forces via laser heating or optical tweezers, the capsule is caused to oscillate. This oscillation creates turbulence in the surrounding fluid, enhancing solute release. Mathematical models, including Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers type equations, describe the oscillating capsule's behavior and identify the optimal oscillation parameter for maximal solute release. Numerical simulations validate theoretical models and highlight two distinct release mechanisms resulting from the turbulence induced by the capsule's oscillation. One mechanism, triggered by the capsule's main oscillation, releases solute near the capsule wall, while another, caused by secondary oscillations, releases solute further away from the wall through shear forces. To quantify the increased solute release due to these mechanisms, a metric known as the'release enhancement factor' is defined and found to significantly increase solute release into the surrounding fluid. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the reliability of causal inferences, and apply it to scenarios with missing outcome data. Through case studies on Facebook's partially-observed conversion events, we develop an approach to conduct large-scale sensitivity analysis by contributing three key improvements. First, we develop a Bayesian estimation technique for sensitivity parameters using unreliable benchmarks that respect data privacy; both objective and subjective initial probability distributions are explored. Second, we leverage the Bayesian estimation of sensitivity parameters to introduce a simulation-based approach for inferring the E-value's posterior distribution. Lastly, we derive closed-form distributions for the E-value that enable direct inference in scenarios where posterior simulation is infeasible due to computational limitations. We showcase improved performance over an existing simulation-based approach in two sub-problems, achieving a speedup of 5.68 times its competitor while achieving equivalent accuracy. We discuss the limitations and potential future solutions for scaling the analysis to thousands of events. Moreover, we release an open-source Python package, called Sensitivity Analyzer, which facilitates data analysis across various industries and domains by enabling users to specify their custom loss functions, benchmark distributions, and posterior inference methods. We demonstrate the framework's capabilities using data from Facebook's conversion events. This research is the first to apply sensitivity analysis to real-world partial observability scenarios, establishing a new analytical framework for drawing causal inferences in such scenarios.

This Feshbach resonance occurs when the bound state within the confined pathway matches the nuclei's relative speed, resulting in divergent cross-sectional measurements. Recent experiments using cold atomic gases have successfully created Feshbach resonances through magnetic field manipulations of a nearby molecular condensate. This has led to observations of properties related to the resonant state, such as increased particle distribution and accelerated flow. In our work, we studied the flow of a bozonic attraction gas near a narrow conical obstacle, creating a controlled Feshbach resonance through variable magnetic field strength. This allowed us to examine the impact of the resonance on both average and maximum flow speeds, using theoretical models and experimental data to describe our findings. This research offers unique insights into understanding matter waves behaving similarly to Schrödinger waves around obstacles. Our formulation, akin to Burer's reformulation but in a lower-dimensional space, generalizes the completely positive matrix cone. We approximate this cone with both inner and outer methods to yield upper and lower bounds, which can seal the optimality gap and thus provide a certificate of exactness beyond established sufficient conditions. We then conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate the quality of the approximations, which in certain cases effectively seal the optimality gap. Additionally, we successfully obtain certificates of exactness for some previously unsolvable instances using our approach. Overall, the performance of the algorithm improves with decreasing dimensionality, and we observe a correlation between the size of the Cholesky factor of the problem matrices and the feasibility of sealing the optimality gap. Consequently, we propose a preprocessing step to reduce the problem size, further enhancing the algorithm's performance. We explore the possibility of linking our approximation method to other established techniques, including conic duality, semidefinite programming, and nuclear norm relaxation. We then illustrate the potential benefits of our approach in nuclear norm relaxation and outline a future research agenda to integrate these methods. Moreover, we extend our reformulation and sealing method to tackle problems with non-convex objectives and completely positive constraints. amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using techniques developed to analyze price indices, they calculated a price-normalized, discipline-specific knowledge index, effectively quantifying the value of new knowledge advancements. Subsequently, they discovered that, on average, each new publication yields around 35% more valuable knowledge than its preceding counterparts. Notably, not all disciplines exhibit the same level of knowledge progression, with mathematics and physics experiencing slower growth (0.5-0.7%) in knowledge progression compared to biology and medicine (1.5-2.5%). These findings suggest that the law of diminishing returns may apply to scientific investments, and that the rate of new knowledge production is unlikely to sustain a perpetual growth trajectory. By providing a systematic knowledge index, this study enables policymakers and funders to evaluate research outcomes more accurately and potentially shift their focus towards emerging areas experiencing faster knowledge progression. Ultimately, the index offers a novel tool for evaluating the dynamics of scientific knowledge and can inform data-driven strategies for advancing scientific progress. The analysis results, along with the associated code, are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ Knowledge

This process involves pre-training a general model on a vast, unlabeled corpus, followed by fine-tuning on datasets of expert-labeled relevance information. The ideal IR system would integrate the perspectives of both users and the system to gauge relevance. The user-centric approach analyzes real users' behavior to determine relevance, whereas the system-centric approach relies on the expertise and signals provided by algorithms. Building on this user-system relevance dichotomy and the success of pre-trained models, this paper proposes Pre-Rank, a novel document ranking framework that harmonizes the two perspectives within a pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm. Specifically, Pre-Rank pre-trains its initial query representations using large datasets of user activity data such as click logs, then fine-tunes these representations with expert-labeled relevance information while incorporating learning-to-rank features under a robust neural network framework. By doing so, Pre-Rank synthesizes the expertise and knowledge of both real search users and IR professionals. The efficacy of Pre-Rank is validated by comparing two implementations based on BERT and SetRank models, which consistently outperformed their respective underlying ranking models by 5.7% and 2.6% in terms of nDCG. While successful in traditional Euclidean environments, there has been limited research exploring backdoor attacks on graph-based data. This study proposes a novel form of backdoor specifically designed for graph data, termed the neighboring backdoor. Due to the unique characteristics of graph data, one significant challenge arises - creating triggers without affecting model accuracy. To address this challenge, we set the trigger as a solitary node. A backdoor, enabled by this node, allows for faulty classification when the connected node falls within predetermined boundaries. We evaluate the neighboring backdoor's effectiveness against existing graph attack methods and present computational evidence confirming its superiority. Furthermore, we demonstrate the flexibility of the neighboring backdoor by showcasing its capability to be implemented both in a white-box and black-box setting. We validate the effectiveness of this attack through computational experiments, which highlight its potential to achieve an attack success rate of up to 85%. To mitigate this threat, we examine existing defense mechanisms and propose a novel approach - neighbor removal - which effectively reduces the attack success rate from 84% to 13.5%. This study paves the way for future research on backdoor attacks within graph data. Data and models used in this research are available at https://github.com/chineseinstitute/Neighboring-Backdoor. A van der Waals-corrected hybrid density functional study found the 8x2 low-temperature hexagonal structure of indium to be energetically preferred over the 4x1 room-temperature configuration. We find that addressing the self-interaction error and incorporating van der Waals interactions significantly contribute to a realistic description of the covalent bonding and energetics within the hexagonal structure. jets are closely linked to the process of mass accretion and provide valuable insights into the development of star formation. Researchers have observed CO and SO emission from the NOEMA telescope directed at the intermediate-mass star-forming system Cep E. Their observations reveal a high-velocity jet composed of knots that originate near the star, surrounded by a slower-moving gas layer. As this gas moves away from the star, its velocity and diameter increase, but its velocity variations remain consistent. Further analysis indicates that the jet breaks up into discrete, moving knots with masses ranging from 1,000 to 100,000 solar masses, moving at varying velocities relative to the star. Studies of these knots and their distributions suggest they form at regular intervals, approximately 50-200 years apart, and their overall mass loss remains relatively steady over time. Researchers propose a precession model to describe the jet dynamics, where the jet and gas around it periodically change direction in response to the star's movement. This precession could be caused by a nearby companion with a mass similar to that of the star, and further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis. As observed jet variability and ejection events in Cep E appear consistent and predictable, these patterns may provide a means to measure distances and other properties in other star-forming systems, particularly those with similar characteristics.
